## 📋 Workshop report

Today, you'll be compiling your first workshop report and using Git/GitHub to post it for peer review using an Issue. Ultimately, it's up to each of you how you format your report; the only requirement is that you utilize a `.qmd` (Quarto Markdown) document to create it. Recall, these are markdown documents that have code chunks that can be run and we can render them as nicely formatted `.html` documents. I highly suggest you use your markdown cheat sheet for help with formatting.

For our purposes, you'll be posting both your `.qmd` and `.html` files for your peer reviewer (tagging the files in your GitHub repository) and then tagging your peer reviewer to assign them to review your code. The process will look like this:

1.  **Complete your report:** Follow the instructions for the workshop and complete your work as a `.qmd` document. Format it appropriately (should be structured, easy-to-follow and your various sections should make clear links to the workshop prompts).
2.  **Stage and commit your changes:** Once you're done with your report, stage and commit your changes locally using an informative commit message.
3.  **Push your changes to GitHub:** Push your changes into your personal course repository.
4.  **Create an issue and assign your reviewer:** In your repository, select the <kbd>Issues</kbd> tab. From there, select <kbd>New issue</kbd>.
    -   Enter a consistent title for each week's submission using this format: `wX_workshop_report` where you replace X with the current week.
    -   See my [example issue here](https://github.com/entomology-3927-5927/hemberger-jeremy-3927/issues/1), and format your issue text similarly. Feel free to add notes to your reviewer (e.g., highlighting areas where you'd like specific feedback or struggled), and include a funny image, meme, or gif because we all need laughs these days. Be sure to tag your reviewer using the `@` sign and selecting their username. Reviewer assignments for each week are posted on the [primary workshop page](workshop-index.qmd).
5.  **Complete your peer review** See the [primary workshop page](workshop-index.qmd) for a peer reviewing rubric and suggestions of what to look for. Remember to be both kind and constructive. No one likes a [Reviewer #2](https://patthomson.net/2026/06/01/how-to-be-reviewer-2/).
6.  **Close the issue:** Once you have completed your peer review, post it, and then mark the issue as "closed".

</br>

## Workshop assignment

### Importing data

1.  Download the `.csv` file for todays lab, and import it into R Studio.

2.  Practice importing the Google Sheets data as well. These data are similarly structured to the `.csv`, but are already cleaned and have additional variables collected.

### Cleaning up data

1.  Inspect the data. You'll find that there are many issues that make these data "untidy".

    Do the column types make sense? Do the column names make sense and are they in the best format to be machine readable?

2.  Clean up the data. This may include:

    -   clean up the column names
    -   adjust how the data for each column are parsed (i.e., their atomic data type) to ensure they'll behave as they're supposed to
    -   account for varying types of missing value codings in the data
    -   ensure your categorical data are consistently coded

::: callout-tip
Some functions that may be of use here are: `janitor::clean_names()`, `mutate()`, `case_when()`, `str_to_lower()`, `readr::parse_number()`, `parse_double()`, `na`, `na_if()`, `replace_with_na()`. Most all of these are in the tidyverse and your cheatsheets but we may not have covered exactly how to use them. Try and figure it out!
:::

3.  Tidy the data. Look at how the tibble is structured. Are these data tidy? If not, use the `pivot_*()` functions to reshape the data appropriately, remembering the rules for tidy data.

### Transforming data

1.  Create a tibble that is a subset of the full data, only including the plot ID, habitat type, species, year, and plant height.

2.  Create a dataset containing only observations from 2026 in restored prairies.

3.  Create a new variable called `height_m` and convert your height appropriately.

4.  Create a new variable called `height_class` that classifies plants as *short* (less than 50 cm), *medium* (50–100 cm), or *tall* (greater than 100 cm). How many observations fall into each class?

5.  Identify the 10 tallest plant observations. Which species, sites, and habitat types do they come from?

### Generate data summaries

1.  Calculate the mean plant height and number of observations for each year. Did average plant height increase or decrease from 2025 to 2026?

2.  Calculate the mean and standard deviation of plant height for each habitat type. Which habitat has the tallest plants on average?

3.  Calculate mean plant height for each species, separately for each year. Which species has the greatest mean height in each year? Are the rankings consistent?
